analysis.quick_summary: Circular motion has tangential velocity and inward radial acceleration because the direction of motion continually changes. Differentiating position in a rotating polar basis gives velocity and the tangential and radial acceleration components. Uniform circular motion has constant speed, but nonzero centripetal acceleration, with equivalent descriptions using angular speed, period, and frequency.

key_concepts.explanation: For a fixed radius r, the position is r⃗(t) = r r̂(t). The outward radial vector r̂ and tangential vector θ̂ rotate with the particle: r̂ = cosθ î + sinθ ĵ and θ̂ = −sinθ î + cosθ ĵ.
Even at constant radius, the basis vectors change direction: d r̂/dt = θ̇ θ̂ and d θ̂/dt = −θ̇ r̂. These identities are essential when differentiating velocity.
The signed tangential component is vθ = rθ̇, so v⃗ = rθ̇ θ̂. Speed is v = r|θ̇|. Distinguish signed angular rate θ̇ from angular speed ω = |θ̇|; the extraction sometimes omits magnitude signs.
A displacement spanning a small positive angle Δθ has chord length 2r sin(Δθ/2). For small angles in radians, this approaches rΔθ. Dividing by Δt and taking the limit gives tangential velocity.
The tangential component is aθ = rθ̈. It arises from changing angular rate and can change the speed.
With outward r̂ positive, ar = −rθ̇². Its magnitude is ac = rω² = v²/r, and it points inward whenever speed is nonzero. The net radial force satisfies Fr = mar.
Zero net tangential force gives aθ = 0 and constant speed. The velocity still changes direction, so acceleration remains inward rather than vanishing.
The period T is the time for one revolution, and frequency f is revolutions per second. For uniform circular motion, T = 2πr/v = 2π/ω and f = 1/T = ω/(2π), measured in hertz.

The inward acceleration magnitude can be written ac = rω² = v²/r = 4π²rf² = 4π²r/T². Choose the form matching the known quantities; do not confuse this positive magnitude with the signed component ar.

For θ(t) = At³ − Bt, θ̇ = 3At² − B and θ̈ = 6At. Thus v⃗ = R(3At² − B)θ̂ and a⃗ = 6RAt θ̂ − R(3At² − B)²r̂. At nonnegative time, centripetal acceleration vanishes at t = √(B/(3A)). The extracted velocity line contains an extra t after B, and the extracted root is missing.

steps.title: Separate fixed radius from changing direction
steps.learning_goal: Describe circular position using a time-dependent polar basis.
steps.explanation: Write r⃗ = r r̂(t) with r fixed. The unit vectors r̂ and θ̂ are perpendicular, but both rotate as θ changes. Their Cartesian sine and cosine expressions show why their time derivatives are not zero.
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the coordinates and directions needed for every subsequent derivative.

steps.title: Derive and visualize tangential velocity
steps.learning_goal: Explain both the direction and magnitude of circular velocity.
steps.explanation: Use d r̂/dt = θ̇θ̂ to obtain v⃗ = rθ̇θ̂. Geometrically, the displacement chord approaches the tangent as Δt approaches zero. Its length approaches r|Δθ|, giving speed v = r|θ̇| = rω. A negative θ̇ reverses the direction without making speed negative.
steps.connection_to_previous: Differentiating the position from the first step turns the rotating radial direction into tangential velocity.

steps.title: Track changes in magnitude and direction
steps.learning_goal: Derive acceleration and interpret its two components.
steps.explanation: Differentiate rθ̇θ̂ using the product rule. Changing θ̇ gives aθ = rθ̈; changing θ̂ gives ar = −rθ̇². The minus sign means inward relative to outward r̂. The net radial force must satisfy Fr = mar. The radial component is zero instantaneously when θ̇ = 0.
steps.connection_to_previous: Velocity changes through its scalar component and its rotating direction, so both must be differentiated.

steps.title: Apply the derivatives to a changing angular rate
steps.learning_goal: Identify when radial acceleration vanishes without assuming total acceleration vanishes.
steps.explanation: For θ = At³ − Bt, calculate θ̇ = 3At² − B and θ̈ = 6At. Therefore vθ = R(3At² − B), aθ = 6RAt, and ar = −R(3At² − B)². For positive A and B, the nonnegative zero-radial-acceleration time is √(B/(3A)); tangential acceleration is still positive there. These derivatives correct the extra t and missing square root in the extracted solution.
steps.connection_to_previous: This example applies the two-component acceleration formula and tests the difference between radial and total acceleration.

steps.title: Specialize to uniform circular motion
steps.learning_goal: Explain why constant speed can coexist with acceleration.
steps.explanation: With zero net tangential force, aθ = 0 and speed remains constant. Velocity is still tangent to a changing point on the circle, so its direction changes. Only the inward acceleration remains, with magnitude ac = rω² = v²/r.
steps.connection_to_previous: After studying variable angular rate, set tangential acceleration to zero to isolate the effect of changing direction.

steps.title: Translate between descriptions of one orbit
steps.learning_goal: Choose an acceleration formula from the available orbital measurements.
steps.explanation: One revolution covers 2πr, so vT = 2πr. Consequently T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T. Substitute these into ac = rω² to obtain ac = 4π²rf² = 4π²r/T². With radius known, any one of v, ω, T, or f determines the others.
steps.connection_to_previous: Constant speed makes the revolution time well defined and connects the uniform-motion acceleration to measurable period and frequency.

analysis.quick_summary: Simple harmonic motion is sinusoidal motion with a repeating period. For a frictionless spring–mass system, the restoring force leads to x″ = −(k/m)x. Verifying sinusoidal solutions gives ω₀ = √(k/m), and combining sine and cosine terms allows the motion to satisfy any initial position and velocity. The same solution can be expressed using amplitude and phase.

key_concepts.explanation: SHM varies sinusoidally. In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), the positive amplitude A sets the extrema +A and −A.
The period T is the repeat time: y(t + T) = y(t). Frequency is f = 1/T in hertz, and angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T = 2πf in rad/s. Angular frequency is constant for SHM.
Displacement x is measured from equilibrium, with positive x indicating extension and negative x compression. The force Fₓ = −kx points toward equilibrium.
Newton’s second law gives mx″ = −kx, or x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction, so it is not constant during nonzero oscillation.
Substituting a cosine solution into the oscillator equation requires ω₀² = k/m. Thus ω₀ = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k). These quantities depend on mass and stiffness, not the initial conditions.
A cos(ω₀t) starts at displacement A with zero velocity. B sin(ω₀t) starts at equilibrium with velocity ω₀B. Each solves the oscillator equation but cannot alone represent all initial conditions.
Because the oscillator equation is linear, sums of its solutions are also solutions. Its general solution is x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
Evaluating position and velocity at t = 0 gives C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. Therefore x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t), valid for any initial position and velocity.

The general solution also equals A cos(ω₀t + φ), with C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ. Hence A = √(C² + D²) = √(x₀² + (vₓ,₀/ω₀)²). The source gives tanφ = −D/C; the coefficient signs must also be used to select the correct quadrant.

The phase is ω₀t + φ and φ is the phase constant. Relative to A cos(ω₀t), positive φ shifts the curve left and negative φ shifts it right. Maxima satisfy ω₀t + φ = 2πn; the n = 0 maximum occurs at t = −φ/ω₀.

steps.title: Read a sinusoidal motion
steps.learning_goal: Distinguish amplitude, period, frequency, and angular frequency.
steps.explanation: In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), A sets the vertical limits and T sets the repeat time. The same curve is A sin(2πft) or A sin(ω₀t), because f = 1/T and ω₀ = 2π/T. Frequency counts cycles per second; angular frequency measures phase advance in rad/s.
steps.connection_to_previous: This foundation establishes the notation needed to describe the spring’s motion.

steps.title: Turn the restoring force into an equation
steps.learning_goal: Explain why spring acceleration is directed toward equilibrium.
steps.explanation: Choose x = 0 at equilibrium and positive x to the right. Extension gives x > 0 and Fₓ < 0; compression gives x < 0 and Fₓ > 0. Substituting Fₓ = −kx into Fₓ = mx″ gives x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration therefore changes with displacement rather than remaining constant.
steps.connection_to_previous: Having described what sinusoidal motion looks like, identify the force law that produces it.

steps.title: Verify the sinusoid and determine its frequency
steps.learning_goal: Derive ω₀ = √(k/m) by matching the equation of motion.
steps.explanation: Try x(t) = A cos(ω₀t). Differentiating twice gives x″ = −ω₀²x, so it satisfies x″ = −(k/m)x when ω₀² = k/m. Thus T = 2π√(m/k). A sine function satisfies the same equation. The extracted text omits some square-root symbols; these roots follow from the stated matching condition.
steps.connection_to_previous: The force equation specifies the required second derivative; the trial sinusoid provides exactly that form.

steps.title: Build a solution flexible enough for any start
steps.learning_goal: Explain why both sine and cosine terms are needed.
steps.explanation: A pure cosine starts with zero velocity, while a pure sine starts at equilibrium. Neither alone covers arbitrary initial position and velocity. Since the differential equation is linear, their sum is also a solution: x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
steps.connection_to_previous: The verified sinusoidal solutions have restricted starting conditions, so combine them to obtain the general form.

steps.title: Fit the motion to initial position and velocity
steps.learning_goal: Determine C and D from x₀ and vₓ,₀.
steps.explanation: Differentiate the general solution to get vₓ(t) = −ω₀C sin(ω₀t) + ω₀D cos(ω₀t). At t = 0, position is C and velocity is ω₀D. Therefore C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀, producing x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t).
steps.connection_to_previous: The general solution has two free coefficients; the two initial conditions fix them.

steps.title: Interpret amplitude and phase
steps.learning_goal: Connect the fitted coefficients to oscillation size and peak timing.
steps.explanation: Expand A cos(ω₀t + φ) and match coefficients: C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ. This gives A = √(C² + D²). Use both coefficient signs to choose φ consistently; the source’s inverse-tangent ratio alone does not resolve its quadrant. Positive φ moves the curve left, negative φ moves it right, and the n = 0 maximum occurs at −φ/ω₀. If both initial conditions are zero, there is no oscillation and phase is unnecessary.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once the initial conditions fix the trajectory, amplitude and phase provide a more direct geometric interpretation of the same solution.

analysis.quick_summary: This lecture derives the constant-input response of an RC circuit using particular and homogeneous solutions. Applying the initial capacitor voltage gives vC(t) = VI + (V0 − VI)e^(−t/RC): the voltage starts at V0 and approaches VI with time constant τ = RC.

key_concepts.explanation: A Thévenin voltage source vI(t) and resistance R drive a capacitor C. The output is the capacitor voltage vC(t).
The node method gives (vC − vI)/R + C dvC/dt = 0, or RC dvC/dt + vC = vI. An initial capacitor voltage is needed to determine the response.
The worked example assumes vI(t) = VI and vC(0) = V0.
A particular solution satisfies the original driven equation. For a constant input, vCP = VI works because its time derivative is zero.
Setting the drive to zero gives RC dvCH/dt + vCH = 0. Trying vCH = Ae^(st) yields s = −1/(RC), so vCH = Ae^(−t/RC).
τ = RC has units of time and sets the exponential response rate. A larger τ produces a slower approach to the final voltage.
Adding the particular and homogeneous solutions gives vC = VI + Ae^(−t/RC). Using vC(0) = V0 determines A = V0 − VI.
The complete response is vC(t) = VI + (V0 − VI)e^(−t/RC). It starts at V0 and approaches VI; the transient is the difference from the final voltage.
iC = C dvC/dt = (VI − V0)e^(−t/RC)/R. The current decays toward zero and its sign depends on whether VI is above or below V0.

For V0 = 0 V and VI = 5 V, the general solution gives 5 − 5e^(−t/RC). For V0 = 5 V and VI = 0 V, it gives 5e^(−t/RC). The charging formula printed on page 8 has a plus-sign error; its plotted curve and stated conditions agree with the minus-sign form.

analysis.quick_summary: Probability calculations depend on how events relate as sets of outcomes. Add probabilities for disjoint events; subtract shared probability when events overlap. Valid probability distributions list disjoint outcomes with probabilities between 0 and 1 that total 1. An event and its complement cover the whole sample space, so their probabilities add to 1.

key_concepts.explanation: A process with uncertain outcomes can be modeled probabilistically, even when its behavior is merely too difficult to predict exactly.
The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes. For one die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a set of outcomes. For example, A = {1, 2} represents rolling either 1 or 2.
Disjoint events have no outcomes in common and cannot occur simultaneously. These two terms mean the same thing.
For disjoint events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). The same principle applies to any collection of mutually disjoint outcomes.
A or B includes outcomes in A, in B, or in both. Statistical 'or' is inclusive unless explicitly stated otherwise.
A and B consists of outcomes belonging to both events. In the card example, the shared outcomes are J♦, Q♦, and K♦.
For any two events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Subtracting the intersection corrects double counting.
A probability distribution lists all disjoint outcomes and their probabilities. Every probability must be between 0 and 1, and the probabilities must sum to 1.
Bar heights represent outcome probabilities. Numerical discrete outcomes can be plotted at their numerical locations, as with two-dice sums.
The complement Aᶜ contains all outcomes in the sample space that are not in A. Since A and Aᶜ are disjoint and exhaustive, P(A) = 1 − P(Aᶜ).

steps.title: Add probabilities when events are disjoint
steps.learning_goal: Recognize no-overlap cases and apply direct addition.
steps.explanation: A = {1, 2} and B = {4, 6} share no outcomes. For the die example, each has probability 1/3, so P(A or B) = 2/3. By contrast, A and D = {2, 3} overlap at outcome 2 and are not disjoint.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once events are written as sets, checking for shared members tells you whether simple addition is valid.

steps.title: Correct double counting for overlapping events
steps.learning_goal: Explain and apply the General Addition Rule.
steps.explanation: Inclusive 'or' includes either event and their intersection. Adding the two event probabilities counts shared outcomes twice, so subtract their probability once. For diamonds or face cards, the result is 13/52 + 12/52 − 3/52 = 22/52. If the intersection is empty, the correction is zero.
steps.connection_to_previous: The general rule extends direct addition to cases where events share outcomes.

steps.title: Check and read a probability distribution
steps.learning_goal: Validate a complete outcome list and interpret its table or plot.
steps.explanation: A distribution must list disjoint outcomes, assign each a probability from 0 to 1, and total 1. The two-dice sum distribution meets these conditions but is not uniform: P(7) = 6/36, while P(2) = P(12) = 1/36. Bar heights show these probabilities.
steps.connection_to_previous: The disjoint-outcome rule now applies to a complete list, whose total probability must account for every possible result.

steps.title: Calculate the easier side using complements
steps.learning_goal: Construct a complement and use it to simplify a probability calculation.
steps.explanation: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and together cover S, so P(A) = 1 − P(Aᶜ). For two dice, the complement of a sum less than 12 is a sum equal to 12. The distribution gives P(12) = 1/36, so P(sum less than 12) = 35/36.

analysis.quick_summary: The excerpt explains how Python operation costs depend on input size, how loop iteration counts combine with the cost of each iteration, and how data structures affect search efficiency. Constant factors can change actual speed without changing growth order. Linear search is O(n), bisection on ordered data is O(log n), and dictionary lookup is described as constant time.

key_concepts.explanation: Big-O describes how work grows with input size, not exact execution time. A faster implementation or a fixed multiplier can change runtime without changing its growth order.
The excerpt treats ordinary arithmetic and sequence or dictionary indexing as constant time. Very large integers are an exception because arithmetic cost grows with their number of digits.
A loop's cost depends on both its iteration count and its body cost. With an O(n^a) body, n or n/k iterations give O(n^(a+1)), while a fixed k iterations give O(n^a), provided k is independent of n.

Traversing all n elements with constant-time work per element is O(n). Both an explicit summation loop and sum are linear, although sum generally has a smaller leading coefficient. min and max are also linear.

Most string and tuple operations are described as linear, with indexing and len as constant-time exceptions. Slicing depends on output length; concatenation depends on the combined operand lengths; join depends on the total length of the strings. Bounded-length string operations are treated as constant time.

Most list methods are described as linear. Appending is O(1) on average because occasional resizing costs are spread over many appends. Removing the last element is constant time, and sorting is O(n log n).

Most dictionary operations are described as constant time. update depends on the size of the incoming dictionary. Creating keys, values, or items iteration objects is described as constant time, but traversing them is linear.

Linear search examines collection items in sequence and stops when it finds the target. Its worst case examines the entire collection, giving O(n). Sequence membership and string methods such as find and count are described as using linear search.

On an ordered sequence, compare the target with the middle item and continue in the appropriate half. Repeated halving gives O(log n); about 20 steps suffice for one million items. Obtaining the required ordering may involve extra work.

Hashtables support search described as constant time without requiring sorted items. Python dictionaries use hashtables, explaining the stated constant-time behavior of dictionary membership and most dictionary operations.

analysis.quick_summary: Effective debugging starts by distinguishing syntax, runtime, and semantic errors. These pages focus on syntax errors: interpret the reported location cautiously, check common structural mistakes, and verify that Python is running the file you actually edited.

key_concepts.explanation: The first debugging task is to identify the kind of error. Syntax, runtime, and semantic errors require different kinds of investigation.
The interpreter detects problems with program structure while translating source code into byte code. A missing colon after a def header is one example.
These occur during execution. Error messages often identify the location and executing functions; infinite recursion can eventually exceed the maximum recursion depth.
A program runs without reporting an error but produces an unintended result. Unexpected expression evaluation order is one possible cause.
A syntax error message identifies where Python noticed a problem, not necessarily where it began. The cause may be on the preceding line.
For incremental development, inspect the most recently added line. For copied code, compare every character while remembering that the reference itself may contain mistakes.

Check reserved keywords, header colons, matching straight quotes, terminated triple-quoted strings, closed delimiters, = versus == in conditionals, consistent indentation, and potentially troublesome pasted characters.

An unterminated triple-quoted string can absorb later code or produce an error far from its origin. An unclosed parenthesis, brace, or bracket makes Python treat the next line as part of the current statement.

If changes have no effect, verify that Python is running the file being edited. A deliberate syntax error near the beginning provides a diagnostic test; if it is not detected, the new code is not being run. Unsaved changes are one possible cause.

analysis.quick_summary: Simple harmonic motion is sinusoidal motion with a repeating period. For a frictionless spring–mass system, the restoring force leads to x″ = −(k/m)x. Verifying sinusoidal solutions gives ω₀ = √(k/m), and combining sine and cosine terms allows the motion to satisfy any initial position and velocity. The same solution can be expressed using amplitude and phase.

key_concepts.explanation: SHM varies sinusoidally. In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), the positive amplitude A sets the extrema +A and −A.
The period T is the repeat time: y(t + T) = y(t). Frequency is f = 1/T in hertz, and angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T = 2πf in rad/s. Angular frequency is constant for SHM.
Displacement x is measured from equilibrium, with positive x indicating extension and negative x compression. The force Fₓ = −kx points toward equilibrium.
Newton’s second law gives mx″ = −kx, or x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction, so it is not constant during nonzero oscillation.
Substituting a cosine solution into the oscillator equation requires ω₀² = k/m. Thus ω₀ = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k). These quantities depend on mass and stiffness, not the initial conditions.
A cos(ω₀t) starts at displacement A with zero velocity. B sin(ω₀t) starts at equilibrium with velocity ω₀B. Each solves the oscillator equation but cannot alone represent all initial conditions.
Because the oscillator equation is linear, sums of its solutions are also solutions. Its general solution is x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
Evaluating position and velocity at t = 0 gives C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. Therefore x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t), valid for any initial position and velocity.

The general solution also equals A cos(ω₀t + φ), with C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ. Hence A = √(C² + D²) = √(x₀² + (vₓ,₀/ω₀)²). The source gives tanφ = −D/C; the coefficient signs must also be used to select the correct quadrant.

The phase is ω₀t + φ and φ is the phase constant. Relative to A cos(ω₀t), positive φ shifts the curve left and negative φ shifts it right. Maxima satisfy ω₀t + φ = 2πn; the n = 0 maximum occurs at t = −φ/ω₀.

analysis.quick_summary: This lecture derives the constant-input response of an RC circuit using particular and homogeneous solutions. Applying the initial capacitor voltage gives vC(t) = VI + (V0 − VI)e^(−t/RC): the voltage starts at V0 and approaches VI with time constant τ = RC.

key_concepts.explanation: A Thévenin voltage source vI(t) and resistance R drive a capacitor C. The output is the capacitor voltage vC(t).
The node method gives (vC − vI)/R + C dvC/dt = 0, or RC dvC/dt + vC = vI. An initial capacitor voltage is needed to determine the response.
The worked example assumes vI(t) = VI and vC(0) = V0.
A particular solution satisfies the original driven equation. For a constant input, vCP = VI works because its time derivative is zero.
Setting the drive to zero gives RC dvCH/dt + vCH = 0. Trying vCH = Ae^(st) yields s = −1/(RC), so vCH = Ae^(−t/RC).
τ = RC has units of time and sets the exponential response rate. A larger τ produces a slower approach to the final voltage.
Adding the particular and homogeneous solutions gives vC = VI + Ae^(−t/RC). Using vC(0) = V0 determines A = V0 − VI.
The complete response is vC(t) = VI + (V0 − VI)e^(−t/RC). It starts at V0 and approaches VI; the transient is the difference from the final voltage.
iC = C dvC/dt = (VI − V0)e^(−t/RC)/R. The current decays toward zero and its sign depends on whether VI is above or below V0.

For V0 = 0 V and VI = 5 V, the general solution gives 5 − 5e^(−t/RC). For V0 = 5 V and VI = 0 V, it gives 5e^(−t/RC). The charging formula printed on page 8 has a plus-sign error; its plotted curve and stated conditions agree with the minus-sign form.

steps.title: Turn the circuit into an equation

steps.explanation: Apply the node method: (vC − vI)/R + C dvC/dt = 0. For constant input VI, this becomes RC dvC/dt + vC = VI, with vC(0) = V0.

steps.title: Find a solution for the constant drive
steps.learning_goal: Verify why vCP = VI is a particular solution.

steps.title: Derive the decaying component
steps.learning_goal: Connect the homogeneous equation to the exponential and time constant.
steps.explanation: Set the drive to zero and try vCH = Ae^(st). Substitution gives RCs + 1 = 0, hence vCH = Ae^(−t/RC). The product τ = RC controls the decay rate.

steps.title: Combine and fit the initial voltage
steps.learning_goal: Determine the transient amplitude from V0.

steps.title: Read the voltage and current behavior
steps.learning_goal: Predict charging, discharging, and the effect of the time constant.
steps.explanation: The voltage starts at V0 and approaches VI. At t = τ, the remaining difference from VI is (V0 − VI)/e. The current is (VI − V0)e^(−t/RC)/R and approaches zero. The worked example assumes vI(t) = VI and vC(0) = V0.
A particular solution satisfies the original driven equation. For a constant input, vCP = VI works because its time derivative is zero.
Setting the drive to zero gives RC dvCH/dt + vCH = 0. Trying vCH = Ae^(st) yields s = −1/(RC), so vCH = Ae^(−t/RC).
τ = RC has units of time and sets the exponential response rate. A larger τ produces a slower approach to the final voltage.
Adding the particular and homogeneous solutions gives vC = VI + Ae^(−t/RC). Using vC(0) = V0 determines A = V0 − VI.
The complete response is vC(t) = VI + (V0 − VI)e^(−t/RC). It starts at V0 and approaches VI; the transient is the difference from the final voltage.
iC = C dvC/dt = (VI − V0)e^(−t/RC)/R. The current decays toward zero and its sign depends on whether VI is above or below V0.

For V0 = 0 V and VI = 5 V, the general solution gives 5 − 5e^(−t/RC). For V0 = 5 V and VI = 0 V, it gives 5e^(−t/RC). The charging formula printed on page 8 has a plus-sign error; its plotted curve and stated conditions agree with the minus-sign form.

analysis.quick_summary: Circular motion has tangential velocity and inward radial acceleration because the direction of motion continually changes. Differentiating position in a rotating polar basis gives velocity and the tangential and radial acceleration components. Uniform circular motion has constant speed, but nonzero centripetal acceleration, with equivalent descriptions using angular speed, period, and frequency.

key_concepts.explanation: For a fixed radius r, the position is r⃗(t) = r r̂(t). The outward radial vector r̂ and tangential vector θ̂ rotate with the particle: r̂ = cosθ î + sinθ ĵ and θ̂ = −sinθ î + cosθ ĵ.
Even at constant radius, the basis vectors change direction: d r̂/dt = θ̇ θ̂ and d θ̂/dt = −θ̇ r̂. These identities are essential when differentiating velocity.
The signed tangential component is vθ = rθ̇, so v⃗ = rθ̇ θ̂. Speed is v = r|θ̇|. Distinguish signed angular rate θ̇ from angular speed ω = |θ̇|; the extraction sometimes omits magnitude signs.
A displacement spanning a small positive angle Δθ has chord length 2r sin(Δθ/2). For small angles in radians, this approaches rΔθ. Dividing by Δt and taking the limit gives tangential velocity.
The tangential component is aθ = rθ̈. It arises from changing angular rate and can change the speed.
With outward r̂ positive, ar = −rθ̇². Its magnitude is ac = rω² = v²/r, and it points inward whenever speed is nonzero. The net radial force satisfies Fr = mar.
Zero net tangential force gives aθ = 0 and constant speed. The velocity still changes direction, so acceleration remains inward rather than vanishing.
The period T is the time for one revolution, and frequency f is revolutions per second. For uniform circular motion, T = 2πr/v = 2π/ω and f = 1/T = ω/(2π), measured in hertz.

The inward acceleration magnitude can be written ac = rω² = v²/r = 4π²rf² = 4π²r/T². Choose the form matching the known quantities; do not confuse this positive magnitude with the signed component ar.

For θ(t) = At³ − Bt, θ̇ = 3At² − B and θ̈ = 6At. Thus v⃗ = R(3At² − B)θ̂ and a⃗ = 6RAt θ̂ − R(3At² − B)²r̂. At nonnegative time, centripetal acceleration vanishes at t = √(B/(3A)). The extracted velocity line contains an extra t after B, and the extracted root is missing.

steps.title: Derive and visualize tangential velocity
steps.learning_goal: Explain both the direction and magnitude of circular velocity.
steps.explanation: Use d r̂/dt = θ̇θ̂ to obtain v⃗ = rθ̇θ̂. Geometrically, the displacement chord approaches the tangent as Δt approaches zero. Its length approaches r|Δθ|, giving speed v = r|θ̇| = rω. A negative θ̇ reverses the direction without making speed negative.

steps.title: Track changes in magnitude and direction
steps.learning_goal: Derive acceleration and interpret its two components.
steps.explanation: Differentiate rθ̇θ̂ using the product rule. Changing θ̇ gives aθ = rθ̈; changing θ̂ gives ar = −rθ̇². The minus sign means inward relative to outward r̂. The net radial force must satisfy Fr = mar. The radial component is zero instantaneously when θ̇ = 0.

steps.title: Apply the derivatives to a changing angular rate
steps.learning_goal: Identify when radial acceleration vanishes without assuming total acceleration vanishes.
steps.explanation: For θ = At³ − Bt, calculate θ̇ = 3At² − B and θ̈ = 6At. Therefore vθ = R(3At² − B), aθ = 6RAt, and ar = −R(3At² − B)². For positive A and B, the nonnegative zero-radial-acceleration time is √(B/(3A)); tangential acceleration is still positive there. steps.title: Specialize to uniform circular motion
steps.learning_goal: Explain why constant speed can coexist with acceleration.
steps.explanation: With zero net tangential force, aθ = 0 and speed remains constant. Velocity is still tangent to a changing point on the circle, so its direction changes. Only the inward acceleration remains, with magnitude ac = rω² = v²/r.
steps.connection_to_previous: After studying variable angular rate, set tangential acceleration to zero to isolate the effect of changing direction.

steps.title: Translate between descriptions of one orbit
steps.learning_goal: Choose an acceleration formula from the available orbital measurements.

analysis.quick_summary: Circular motion has tangential velocity and inward radial acceleration because the direction of motion continually changes. Differentiating position in a rotating polar basis gives velocity and the tangential and radial acceleration components. Uniform circular motion has constant speed, but nonzero centripetal acceleration, with equivalent descriptions using angular speed, period, and frequency.

key_concepts.explanation: For a fixed radius r, the position is r⃗(t) = r r̂(t). The outward radial vector r̂ and tangential vector θ̂ rotate with the particle: r̂ = cosθ î + sinθ ĵ and θ̂ = −sinθ î + cosθ ĵ.
Even at constant radius, the basis vectors change direction: d r̂/dt = θ̇ θ̂ and d θ̂/dt = −θ̇ r̂. These identities are essential when differentiating velocity.
The signed tangential component is vθ = rθ̇, so v⃗ = rθ̇ θ̂. Speed is v = r|θ̇|. Distinguish signed angular rate θ̇ from angular speed ω = |θ̇|; the extraction sometimes omits magnitude signs.
A displacement spanning a small positive angle Δθ has chord length 2r sin(Δθ/2). For small angles in radians, this approaches rΔθ. Dividing by Δt and taking the limit gives tangential velocity.
The tangential component is aθ = rθ̈. It arises from changing angular rate and can change the speed.
With outward r̂ positive, ar = −rθ̇². Its magnitude is ac = rω² = v²/r, and it points inward whenever speed is nonzero. The net radial force satisfies Fr = mar.
Zero net tangential force gives aθ = 0 and constant speed. The velocity still changes direction, so acceleration remains inward rather than vanishing.
The period T is the time for one revolution, and frequency f is revolutions per second. For uniform circular motion, T = 2πr/v = 2π/ω and f = 1/T = ω/(2π), measured in hertz.

The inward acceleration magnitude can be written ac = rω² = v²/r = 4π²rf² = 4π²r/T². Choose the form matching the known quantities; do not confuse this positive magnitude with the signed component ar.

For θ(t) = At³ − Bt, θ̇ = 3At² − B and θ̈ = 6At. Thus v⃗ = R(3At² − B)θ̂ and a⃗ = 6RAt θ̂ − R(3At² − B)²r̂. At nonnegative time, centripetal acceleration vanishes at t = √(B/(3A)). The extracted velocity line contains an extra t after B, and the extracted root is missing.

analysis.quick_summary: Effective debugging starts by distinguishing syntax, runtime, and semantic errors. These pages focus on syntax errors: interpret the reported location cautiously, check common structural mistakes, and verify that Python is running the file you actually edited.

key_concepts.explanation: The first debugging task is to identify the kind of error. Syntax, runtime, and semantic errors require different kinds of investigation.

A program runs without reporting an error but produces an unintended result. Unexpected expression evaluation order is one possible cause.
A syntax error message identifies where Python noticed a problem, not necessarily where it began. The cause may be on the preceding line.
For incremental development, inspect the most recently added line. For copied code, compare every character while remembering that the reference itself may contain mistakes.

analysis.quick_summary: Simple harmonic motion is sinusoidal motion with a repeating period. For a frictionless spring–mass system, the restoring force leads to x″ = −(k/m)x. Verifying sinusoidal solutions gives ω₀ = √(k/m), and combining sine and cosine terms allows the motion to satisfy any initial position and velocity. The same solution can be expressed using amplitude and phase.

key_concepts.explanation: SHM varies sinusoidally. In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), the positive amplitude A sets the extrema +A and −A.
The period T is the repeat time: y(t + T) = y(t). Frequency is f = 1/T in hertz, and angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T = 2πf in rad/s. Angular frequency is constant for SHM.
Displacement x is measured from equilibrium, with positive x indicating extension and negative x compression. The force Fₓ = −kx points toward equilibrium.
Newton’s second law gives mx″ = −kx, or x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction, so it is not constant during nonzero oscillation.
Substituting a cosine solution into the oscillator equation requires ω₀² = k/m. Thus ω₀ = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k). These quantities depend on mass and stiffness, not the initial conditions.
A cos(ω₀t) starts at displacement A with zero velocity. B sin(ω₀t) starts at equilibrium with velocity ω₀B. Each solves the oscillator equation but cannot alone represent all initial conditions.
Because the oscillator equation is linear, sums of its solutions are also solutions. Its general solution is x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
Evaluating position and velocity at t = 0 gives C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. Therefore x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t), valid for any initial position and velocity.

The general solution also equals A cos(ω₀t + φ), with C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ. Hence A = √(C² + D²) = √(x₀² + (vₓ,₀/ω₀)²). The source gives tanφ = −D/C; the coefficient signs must also be used to select the correct quadrant.

The phase is ω₀t + φ and φ is the phase constant. Relative to A cos(ω₀t), positive φ shifts the curve left and negative φ shifts it right. Maxima satisfy ω₀t + φ = 2πn; the n = 0 maximum occurs at t = −φ/ω₀.

steps.title: Turn the restoring force into an equation

analysis.quick_summary: Simple harmonic motion is sinusoidal motion with a repeating period. For a frictionless spring–mass system, the restoring force leads to x″ = −(k/m)x. Verifying sinusoidal solutions gives ω₀ = √(k/m), and combining sine and cosine terms allows the motion to satisfy any initial position and velocity. key_concepts.explanation: SHM varies sinusoidally. In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), the positive amplitude A sets the extrema +A and −A.
The period T is the repeat time: y(t + T) = y(t). Frequency is f = 1/T in hertz, and angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T = 2πf in rad/s. Angular frequency is constant for SHM.
Displacement x is measured from equilibrium, with positive x indicating extension and negative x compression. The force Fₓ = −kx points toward equilibrium.
Newton’s second law gives mx″ = −kx, or x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction, so it is not constant during nonzero oscillation.
Substituting a cosine solution into the oscillator equation requires ω₀² = k/m. Thus ω₀ = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k). These quantities depend on mass and stiffness, not the initial conditions.
A cos(ω₀t) starts at displacement A with zero velocity. B sin(ω₀t) starts at equilibrium with velocity ω₀B. Each solves the oscillator equation but cannot alone represent all initial conditions.
Because the oscillator equation is linear, sums of its solutions are also solutions. Its general solution is x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
Evaluating position and velocity at t = 0 gives C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. Therefore x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t), valid for any initial position and velocity.

The general solution also equals A cos(ω₀t + φ), with C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ. Hence A = √(C² + D²) = √(x₀² + (vₓ,₀/ω₀)²). The source gives tanφ = −D/C; the coefficient signs must also be used to select the correct quadrant.

The phase is ω₀t + φ and φ is the phase constant. Relative to A cos(ω₀t), positive φ shifts the curve left and negative φ shifts it right. Maxima satisfy ω₀t + φ = 2πn; the n = 0 maximum occurs at t = −φ/ω₀.

steps.title: Read a sinusoidal motion
steps.learning_goal: Distinguish amplitude, period, frequency, and angular frequency.
steps.explanation: In y(t) = A sin(2πt/T), A sets the vertical limits and T sets the repeat time. The same curve is A sin(2πft) or A sin(ω₀t), because f = 1/T and ω₀ = 2π/T. Frequency counts cycles per second; angular frequency measures phase advance in rad/s.

steps.title: Turn the restoring force into an equation
steps.learning_goal: Explain why spring acceleration is directed toward equilibrium.
steps.explanation: Choose x = 0 at equilibrium and positive x to the right. Extension gives x > 0 and Fₓ < 0; compression gives x < 0 and Fₓ > 0. Substituting Fₓ = −kx into Fₓ = mx″ gives x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration therefore changes with displacement rather than remaining constant.
steps.connection_to_previous: Having described what sinusoidal motion looks like, identify the force law that produces it.

steps.title: Verify the sinusoid and determine its frequency
steps.learning_goal: Derive ω₀ = √(k/m) by matching the equation of motion.
steps.explanation: Try x(t) = A cos(ω₀t). Differentiating twice gives x″ = −ω₀²x, so it satisfies x″ = −(k/m)x when ω₀² = k/m. Thus T = 2π√(m/k). A sine function satisfies the same equation. The extracted text omits some square-root symbols; these roots follow from the stated matching condition.
steps.connection_to_previous: The force equation specifies the required second derivative; the trial sinusoid provides exactly that form.

steps.title: Build a solution flexible enough for any start

steps.explanation: A pure cosine starts with zero velocity, while a pure sine starts at equilibrium. Neither alone covers arbitrary initial position and velocity. Since the differential equation is linear, their sum is also a solution: x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
steps.connection_to_previous: The verified sinusoidal solutions have restricted starting conditions, so combine them to obtain the general form.

steps.title: Fit the motion to initial position and velocity
steps.learning_goal: Determine C and D from x₀ and vₓ,₀.

key_concepts.explanation: A process with uncertain outcomes can be modeled probabilistically, even when its behavior is merely too difficult to predict exactly.
The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes. For one die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a set of outcomes. For example, A = {1, 2} represents rolling either 1 or 2.
Disjoint events have no outcomes in common and cannot occur simultaneously. These two terms mean the same thing.

A probability distribution lists all disjoint outcomes and their probabilities. Every probability must be between 0 and 1, and the probabilities must sum to 1.
Bar heights represent outcome probabilities. Numerical discrete outcomes can be plotted at their numerical locations, as with two-dice sums.

steps.title: Identify the sample space and events
steps.learning_goal: Distinguish all possible outcomes from a selected set of outcomes.
steps.explanation: For one die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. An event selects outcomes from S, such as A = {1, 2}. Event membership is the foundation for deciding whether events overlap.
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the set language needed for every later probability rule.

steps.title: Add probabilities when events are disjoint
steps.learning_goal: Recognize no-overlap cases and apply direct addition.
steps.explanation: A = {1, 2} and B = {4, 6} share no outcomes. For the die example, each has probability 1/3, so P(A or B) = 2/3. By contrast, A and D = {2, 3} overlap at outcome 2 and are not disjoint.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once events are written as sets, checking for shared members tells you whether simple addition is valid.

steps.title: Correct double counting for overlapping events
steps.learning_goal: Explain and apply the General Addition Rule.
steps.explanation: Inclusive 'or' includes either event and their intersection. Adding the two event probabilities counts shared outcomes twice, so subtract their probability once. For diamonds or face cards, the result is 13/52 + 12/52 − 3/52 = 22/52. If the intersection is empty, the correction is zero.
steps.connection_to_previous: The general rule extends direct addition to cases where events share outcomes.

steps.title: Check and read a probability distribution
steps.learning_goal: Validate a complete outcome list and interpret its table or plot.
steps.explanation: A distribution must list disjoint outcomes, assign each a probability from 0 to 1, and total 1. The two-dice sum distribution meets these conditions but is not uniform: P(7) = 6/36, while P(2) = P(12) = 1/36. Bar heights show these probabilities.
steps.connection_to_previous: The disjoint-outcome rule now applies to a complete list, whose total probability must account for every possible result.

steps.title: Calculate the easier side using complements
steps.learning_goal: Construct a complement and use it to simplify a probability calculation.
steps.explanation: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and together cover S, so P(A) = 1 − P(Aᶜ). For two dice, the complement of a sum less than 12 is a sum equal to 12. The distribution gives P(12) = 1/36, so P(sum less than 12) = 35/36.

steps.title: Correct double counting for overlapping events
steps.learning_goal: Explain and apply the General Addition Rule.
steps.explanation: Inclusive 'or' includes either event and their intersection. Adding the two event probabilities counts shared outcomes twice, so subtract their probability once. For diamonds or face cards, the result is 13/52 + 12/52 − 3/52 = 22/52. If the intersection is empty, the correction is zero.

analysis.quick_summary: The excerpt explains how Python operation costs depend on input size, how loop iteration counts combine with the cost of each iteration, and how data structures affect search efficiency. Constant factors can change actual speed without changing growth order. Linear search is O(n), bisection on ordered data is O(log n), and dictionary lookup is described as constant time.

key_concepts.explanation: Big-O describes how work grows with input size, not exact execution time. A faster implementation or a fixed multiplier can change runtime without changing its growth order.
The excerpt treats ordinary arithmetic and sequence or dictionary indexing as constant time. Very large integers are an exception because arithmetic cost grows with their number of digits.
A loop's cost depends on both its iteration count and its body cost. With an O(n^a) body, n or n/k iterations give O(n^(a+1)), while a fixed k iterations give O(n^a), provided k is independent of n.

Traversing all n elements with constant-time work per element is O(n). Both an explicit summation loop and sum are linear, although sum generally has a smaller leading coefficient. min and max are also linear.

Most string and tuple operations are described as linear, with indexing and len as constant-time exceptions. Slicing depends on output length; concatenation depends on the combined operand lengths; join depends on the total length of the strings. Bounded-length string operations are treated as constant time.

Most list methods are described as linear. Appending is O(1) on average because occasional resizing costs are spread over many appends. Removing the last element is constant time, and sorting is O(n log n).

Most dictionary operations are described as constant time. update depends on the size of the incoming dictionary. Creating keys, values, or items iteration objects is described as constant time, but traversing them is linear.

Linear search examines collection items in sequence and stops when it finds the target. Its worst case examines the entire collection, giving O(n). Sequence membership and string methods such as find and count are described as using linear search.

On an ordered sequence, compare the target with the middle item and continue in the appropriate half. Repeated halving gives O(log n); about 20 steps suffice for one million items. Obtaining the required ordering may involve extra work.

Hashtables support search described as constant time without requiring sorted items. Python dictionaries use hashtables, explaining the stated constant-time behavior of dictionary membership and most dictionary operations.
